title: Loveland Well Depth and Drilling Cost Guide
meta_description: Loveland wells have a 27-foot median depth; local drilling and completed-well costs vary with fractured mountain bedrock.
h1: What Loveland Wells Cost, Produce, and Require
intro_html:
This guide covers permitted wells within 5 miles of Loveland in Larimer County. The records include 1,298 wells, but only 457 are recorded as constructed, 738 report total depth, 54 report pump yield, and 30 report static water level. That uneven reporting matters: the numbers are useful for local planning, but they are not a guarantee for a particular lot.

Loveland sits in a mountain setting where many permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Nearby Windsor, Fort Collins, Timnath, Berthoud, Johnstown, and Milliken can provide broader context, but a buyer should give the most weight to wells close to the property and in the same geologic setting.

sections.heading: Loveland well depths: shallow records with deeper exceptions
sections.html:
The recorded median well depth near Loveland is 27 feet. The middle half runs from 20 to 49 feet, so many local drilling bids may look modest compared with mountain areas where bedrock wells extend much farther. Still, the shallow median does not define every parcel.

87% of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 7% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 4% between 300 and 600 feet, and 1% exceed 600 feet. The 90th percentile is 137 feet, and the deepest record reaches 700 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss can change abruptly across short distances, so use nearby well logs to frame a bid rather than relying on the median alone.

sections.heading: How much water a Loveland well may produce
sections.html:
Among the limited pump-yield records, the median is 9.7 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 1.5 to 15.0 gallons per minute. That spread is important for a home buyer: a well near the low end may require careful household use and storage planning, while a stronger well gives more operating room.

The records show 19% under 1 gallon per minute, 11% from 1 to 5, 37% from 5 to 15, and 33% above 15 gallons per minute. A yield under 1 gallon per minute is not automatically unusable, but it deserves a professional assessment of recharge, storage, fixtures, and intended use. Confirm the actual test method and duration before comparing wells.

sections.heading: Loveland water levels and what the records suggest
sections.html:
Reported static water levels are generally shallow in this dataset. The median depth to water is 11 feet, with the middle half between 8 and 20 feet below the surface. That can reduce pumping lift, but it also means shallow groundwater may be more exposed to surface conditions.

The decade summaries do not show a simple falling water table: the median reported level was 18 feet below surface in the 2010s and 8 feet in the 2020s. A smaller depth means water was measured closer to the surface, not farther down. Only 30 wells report static water level, so treat this as a limited permit-record signal rather than a basin-wide trend. A current measurement on the property is more useful for a purchase decision.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Loveland, and how active permits are
sections.html:
Permit activity spans several generations. Records show 26 permits from the 1950s, 8 from the 1960s, 41 from the 1970s, 110 from the 1980s, 261 from the 1990s, 176 from the 2000s, 200 from the 2010s, and 99 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most frequent driller names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 367 records, Boyles Bros. Drilling Co. (Lensch, George E) with 75, and Drilling Engineers Inc. (Smith, Chester C.) with 51. These names show local record history, not a guarantee of current availability or performance. Check the Colorado DWR permit and construction documents before treating an old log as comparable.

sections.heading: What a new Loveland well may cost to drill
sections.html:
Local cost planning is based on fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The drilling rate is typically $65 to $100 per foot. At the recorded median depth of 27 feet, the drilled hole is modeled at about $1,800 to $2,700.

That is only the hole. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $7,800 to $14,700. A contractor’s proposal can move outside that range when access, casing, grout, difficult rock, water testing, or site conditions add work. Ask what is included and how the price changes if the driller must continue below the expected depth. Fractured-bedrock production is unpredictable, so keep a contingency and do not compare bids by footage alone.

sections.heading: Loveland risks: water quality, yield, septic, and building plans
sections.html:
Permit records name the unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer for 1,040 wells, with 61 in the Pierre Shale and 55 in alluvial material. No wells in this dataset are identified in the Denver Basin aquifer. Groundwater conditions can differ by formation and by lot, so test the water rather than assuming a neighboring result applies.

Within about 10 miles, the map includes 274 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 38 historic mine features, and 9 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped sites do not prove contamination at a home, but they justify a records review and laboratory testing. Also check well separation from septic systems, available building envelopes, driveway access, casing and grout details, and whether the intended use fits the permit. Domestic or household use accounts for 22% of permits; monitoring accounts for 50%.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Loveland well lot
sections.html:
Before closing, obtain the well permit, construction report, pump-yield test, static water level, and recent water-quality results if they exist. Compare the property with nearby records, especially wells in the same fractured-rock setting. A local median of 27 feet and 9.7 gallons per minute helps frame expectations, but the reported range includes low-producing wells and records as deep as 700 feet.

For a new build, confirm the water right or exempt-well status with Colorado DWR, the permitted uses, and any limits that apply. An exempt household-use well generally has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required. Have the driller and excavation contractor review access, staging, trench routes, septic placement, electrical service, and the building site together before you commit to plans.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Loveland, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth is 27 feet, and the middle half runs from 20 to 49 feet. Most, or 87%, are under 100 feet. Conditions still vary sharply in fractured granite and gneiss: the deepest record is 700 feet, and the 90th percentile is 137 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Loveland?
faq.a: The modeled drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 27 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at $1,800 to $2,700. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $7,800 to $14,700. Rock, access, and added depth can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a Loveland well produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 9.7 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 1.5 to 15.0. The records show 19% under 1 gallon per minute and 33% above 15. Only 54 wells report yield, so request a current, documented pump test for the property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Loveland?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a well’s depth or yield. Within about 10 miles are 274 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 38 historic mine features, and 9 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These locations do not establish contamination at your lot. Test the well through a qualified laboratory and review nearby environmental records before drinking the water.

faq.q: Do Loveland wells have a falling water table?
faq.a: The available records do not show a simple falling trend. Median reported depth to water was 18 feet below surface in the 2010s and 8 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later median was shallower. The sample is limited to 30 wells with static water-level data, so measure the property’s current water level rather than relying on the decade comparison.
